newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia optimistic on merger with guerrillas.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia optimistic on merger with guerrillas.

text.p: Cambodian military leaders said on Monday they were optimistic that dissident Khmer Rouge guerrillas would soon merge with the armed forces and could be in government uniforms within a week.

Lieutenant General Nhek Bun Chhay, armed forces deputy chief of staff and one of the top government negotiators in talks with the breakaway faction, told Reuters that the guerrillas had agreed to government demands on merging forces at a meeting in the northwest city of Battambang on Friday.

"There are no more meetings for negotiation, but there is only the implementation of the decision (to merge forces)," said the general, who believed the guerrillas would be wearing royal armed forces uniforms later this week.

Co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen met top armed forces officers at the defence ministry on Monday to explain government plans for the merger with the guerrillas loyal to Ieng Sary, Ranariddh told reporters.
Ieng Sary, foreign minister during the Khmer Rouge's brutal 1975-79 rule, broke from the mainstream guerrillas in early August and forged a ceasefire with the government.
The two sides began military merger talks after Ieng Sary received a royal pardon on September 14 for his role in the genocide of more than one million people under the Maoist regime.

The guerrillas asked for top central command posts in the police and military and demanded that their Pailin base in northwest Cambodia become the centre of a new province and remain under their control.

Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, apparently angered by the demands, said last Friday the guerrillas must merge forces with the government immediately and drop plans to govern a separate state or face possible arrest.

Top military officers presented the government demands to Ieng Sary's senior commanders on Friday and they were accepted, Ranariddh said on Saturday, adding that senior regional military posts would be given to the dissidents.
The prince told reporters on Monday he had received word that Ieng Sary still intended to join forces with the government.

The Khmer Rouge signed a U.N.-brokered peace accord with rival factions in 1991 but later reneged on the pact. The faction had been fighting the coalition government that emerged from elections in 1993 until it was crippled by last month's split.
